# Fitting Functions

## `fit()`

The primary estimation entry point. Runs FOCE, FOCEI, or SAEM depending on `options.method`.

```rust
pub fn fit(
    model: &CompiledModel,
    population: &Population,
    init_params: &ModelParameters,
    options: &FitOptions,
) -> Result<FitResult, String>
```

**Parameters:**
- `model`: Compiled model from `parse_model_file()` or `parse_full_model_file()`
- `population`: Population data from `read_population_for()` (or `read_nonmem_csv()` for a Gaussian-only model — see [Parsing](parsing.qmd#read_nonmem_csv))
- `init_params`: Initial parameter values
- `options`: Estimation configuration

**Returns:** `FitResult` with parameter estimates, standard errors, and per-subject diagnostics.

**Example:**
```rust
use ferx_core::api::read_population_for;

let model = parse_model_file(Path::new("model.ferx"))?;
let (population, _) = read_population_for(&model, &None, "data.csv", None, None, None, &[])?;
let options = FitOptions::default();

let result = fit(&model, &population, &model.default_params, &options)?;
println!("OFV: {:.4}", result.ofv);
```

A model with a data-driven level block (`theta NAME[COL, ...]`) or a symbolic
`[covariate_model]` statistic needs one more step between reading and fitting.
See [Assembling the inputs yourself](#assembling-the-inputs-yourself).

## `fit_from_files()`

Convenience wrapper that handles parsing and data reading. `data_path` is
`None` to rely solely on the model's own `[data]` block (see
[data.qmd](../model-file/data.qmd)); when both are given, `data_path`
overrides the model's, with a warning recorded on the result.

```rust
pub fn fit_from_files(
    model_path: &str,
    data_path: Option<&str>,
    covariate_columns: Option<&[&str]>,
    options: Option<FitOptions>,
) -> Result<FitResult, String>
```

**Example:**
```rust
let result = fit_from_files(
    "model.ferx",
    Some("data.csv"),
    None,          // Auto-detect covariates
    None,          // Default options
)?;
```

## `run_model_with_data()`

Full pipeline: parse model file, read data, fit. Returns both the fit result and the population.
`data_path` is `None` to rely solely on the model's own `[data]` block.

```rust
pub fn run_model_with_data(
    model_path: &str,
    data_path: Option<&str>,
) -> Result<(FitResult, Population), String>
```

Uses the `[fit_options]` from the model file.

## `run_model_simulate()`

Simulation-estimation: parse model, generate data from `[simulation]` block, fit.

```rust
pub fn run_model_simulate(
    model_path: &str,
) -> Result<(FitResult, Population), String>
```

Requires a `[simulation]` block in the model file.

## Running many fits

A tool that runs hundreds of fits (bootstrap, SCM, model search) has two things
to get right that a single interactive fit does not: how the thread budget is
split, and how much each fit prints.

### Splitting the thread budget (`PoolPlan`)

`fit()` already parallelises over subjects, so a naive outer `par_iter` over
replicates nests one Rayon pool on top of another and the two levels compete
for the same workers. `PoolPlan` makes the split explicit and builds the outer
pool correctly:

```rust
use ferx_core::{fit, FitOptions, PoolPlan};

// 200 replicates on an 8-thread budget: 8 fits at a time, each single-threaded.
let plan = PoolPlan::from_budget(8, 200);
assert_eq!((plan.replicates(), plan.threads_per_fit()), (8, 1));

let mut options = FitOptions::default().quiet();
plan.apply_to(&mut options);          // sets FitOptions::threads

let results: Vec<_> = plan.install(|| {
    use rayon::prelude::*;
    (0..200).into_par_iter().map(|_i| fit(&model, &population, &init, &options)).collect()
})?;
```

The budget is spent on the outer level first, because replicate-level
parallelism is embarrassingly parallel while the per-subject level synchronises
every iteration:

```text
replicates      = min(total_threads, n_units)     (at least 1)
threads_per_fit = total_threads / replicates      (at least 1, floored)
```

So `from_budget(8, 200)` is `8 x 1`, `from_budget(8, 2)` is `2 x 4`, and
`from_budget(8, 3)` is `3 x 2` — the division floors rather than
oversubscribing. `total_threads = 0` means the engine default (available cores
minus one, capped at 8); both levels are always at least 1, so a plan never
silently means "let Rayon decide".

`PoolPlan::install()` is the part you should not hand-roll. ferx builds its own
pools with a 32 MiB worker stack (`FIT_RAYON_STACK_SIZE`) because wide ODE+IOV
analytic-gradient models overflow the platform-default 2 MiB Rayon stack. An
outer pool built from a bare `rayon::ThreadPoolBuilder::new()` inherits that
default and faults on exactly the models that need the bigger stack — and only
under a tool, where nothing else looks.

With `threads_per_fit == 1`, `apply_to()` gives the documented single-threaded
inner mode: the fit runs its per-subject loops on a one-worker pool and reports
`n_threads_used == 1`. Estimates do not depend on the thread count — the
per-subject likelihood is reduced in subject order — so a replicate fitted on
one thread is bit-identical to the same replicate fitted on four.

### Quiet fits

`FitOptions::verbose` defaults to `true`, which suits one interactive fit and is
unusable for 200 of them. `FitOptions::quiet()` turns it off:

```rust
let options = FitOptions { outer_maxiter: 200, ..Default::default() }.quiet();
```

A quiet fit writes nothing to stdout or stderr. Nothing is lost: every non-fatal
message the engine produces goes into `FitResult::warnings` (and
`warnings_structured`) regardless of `verbose`, so the tool reads them off each
result and prints its own one-line-per-replicate progress instead.

## Ranking candidates: BIC variants and strictness

A search (covariate, structural, variability — the #1175 tools) is *generate a
candidate → fit it → rank it*. Two things the ranking step needs live in
`ferx-core` (#1177): the BIC convention to rank on, and a gate that decides
whether a candidate's fit is trustworthy enough to be ranked at all.

### BIC variants (`bic`)

`FitResult::bic` is the classical `OFV + p · ln(n_obs)`. Pharmpy's `iivsearch`
and `modelsearch` rank on the Delattre et al. (2014) **mixed** BIC instead, which
penalises the *random-effects class* of parameters on `ln(n_subjects)` and the
rest on `ln(n_obs)` — ranking IIV structures on the observation-count BIC
systematically favours the wrong model. `bic()` gives all four of
`pharmpy.modeling.calculate_bic`'s variants from a finished `FitResult`:

```rust
use ferx_core::{bic, BicType};

let mixed  = bic(&result, BicType::Mixed);   // Pharmpy's default
let iiv    = bic(&result, BicType::Iiv);     // free Ω elements only, ln(n_subjects)
let random = bic(&result, BicType::Random);  // every parameter on ln(n_subjects)
let fixed  = bic(&result, BicType::Fixed);   // == result.bic
```

| `BicType` | penalty |
|---|---|
| `Mixed` | `n_random · ln(n_subjects) + n_fixed · ln(n_obs)` |
| `Iiv` | `n_omega · ln(n_subjects)` |
| `Random` | `n_parameters · ln(n_subjects)` |
| `Fixed` | `n_parameters · ln(n_obs)` |

Class membership follows Pharmpy: every free Ω / Ω_IOV element is random; a θ
is random when it reaches — directly or through intermediate
`[individual_parameters]` assignments — a parameter expression that carries an
ETA or KAPPA, and fixed otherwise; σ (and a `block_sigma` correlation) is fixed
unless the residual error itself carries an ETA (`iiv_on_ruv`). The
`[event_model]`, `[binary_model]` and `[markov_model]` expressions count too,
since they accept ETA directly: `scale = TVSCALE * exp(ETA_SCALE)` in a TTE-only
model with no `[individual_parameters]` makes `TVSCALE` random-class, the same
as writing that line as an individual parameter. (A θ that meets its η only in a
Form-C `y = …` readout or an `[odes]` hazard line is not seen and stays
fixed-class.) A `[covariate_nn]`'s weights are θ too: an output head read
through an η-bearing parameter (`CL = TYPICAL_PK.CL * exp(ETA_CL)`) makes the
shared hidden-layer weights and that head's row and bias random-class, while
another head's own weights stay fixed-class. The tally is recorded on
`FitResult::bic_inputs` at fit time, so a
`.fitrx` bundle can be ranked without re-parsing the model; a bundle saved
before the tally existed gets `NaN` rather than a wrong penalty.

The four variants are pinned in unit tests to `calculate_bic()`'s own outputs
on Pharmpy's `pheno` example (59 subjects, 155 observations, three θ that all
reach an η-bearing parameter, two Ω, one σ): mixed 611.707, fixed 616.537,
random 610.741, iiv 594.431.

### Strictness (`check_strictness`)

`FitResult::converged` is a bool. It is never `true` at an objective that is not
a usable number — `NaN`, infinite, or the clamped divergence sentinel all report
`converged: false` with a `W_NONFINITE_OBJECTIVE` warning (#1303) — but it does
not distinguish a genuine optimum from an init stall (#751), a boundary estimate,
an ill-conditioned covariance step or a near-singular correlation matrix. Under automation every one of those becomes
a *model-selection error*: a candidate that never left its initial estimates is
ranked on an OFV that says nothing about the model. `Strictness` is the
pyDarwin-style gate, and the verdict carries the *reasons*, so a search report
can say why a candidate was excluded instead of silently dropping it:

```rust
use ferx_core::{check_strictness, Strictness};

let gate = Strictness {
    require_covariance: true,
    ..Strictness::default()
};
let verdict = check_strictness(&result, &gate);
if !verdict.passed {
    for reason in &verdict.failures {
        eprintln!("excluded: {reason}");
    }
}
```

| field | default | fails when |
|---|---|---|
| `require_converged` | `true` | `converged == false` — which also covers an internal runaway-guard hit, and a [non-finite objective](../warnings.qmd#non-finite-objective) (`NaN`, infinite, or the clamped divergence sentinel), both of which demote `converged` |
| `require_covariance` | `false` | the covariance step did not run or failed. A SIR fallback that delivered credible intervals is accepted — unless its importance weights collapsed onto a single draw (Kish ESS below 2, every interval of zero width), which fails like a failed step; an accepted fallback stores no matrix, so the threshold gates below then report `skipped` |
| `max_condition_number` | `Some(1000)` | `cov_condition_number` exceeds it (∞ for a singular correlation matrix) |
| `max_correlation` | `Some(0.95)` | any off-diagonal of the covariance's correlation form exceeds it in absolute value — the whole matrix, not just θ, read on the natural scale (a `block_omega` / block-κ segment is mapped off its Cholesky coordinates by the delta method first, so the number is the ω correlation NONMEM's `.cor` would show — the layout comes from `FitResult::omega_is_diagonal` / `kappa_is_diagonal`, and a bundle saved before those were recorded is read as stored); the offending pair is named by its packed coordinate (`CL ~ log_chol_ETA_CL`) |
| `reject_on_boundary` | `true` | a θ is pinned to a declared bound — the same predicate `bootstrap`'s `skip_estimate_near_boundary` applies |
| `reject_init_stall` | `true` | the fit never left its initial estimates (the #751 signature): the outer optimizer's own escape verdict when the result carries it (`FitResult::left_init`, recorded by the NLopt outer loop), otherwise no free θ/Ω/σ moved more than 1 % of its initial value; a fit with `n_parameters == 0` cannot stall, and one whose only free coordinates are κ / mixture / `block_sigma` entries with no optimizer verdict is `skipped`. This assumes a **cold start** — a candidate warm-started from its parent's estimates legitimately converges where it began, so turn the gate off for such a search |

While either threshold is enabled, a fit whose covariance step had to floor a
Hessian eigenvalue — the `Covariance step regularized: eigenvalue floor applied …`
[`covariance_regularized`](../warnings.qmd#codes-convergence) warning — fails
as well (#1512); the non-finite cross-partial note that shares that code does
not. The floor replaces a direction of negative or
near-zero curvature with a finite one, so the matrix both thresholds read no
longer shows the problem: a collapsed peripheral compartment (V2 → 0, Q free)
on warfarin read a condition number of 2.98 next to a TVQ RSE of 293519 %, and
passed. The floor fires only when the Hessian is indefinite or its smallest
eigenvalue is below `1e-10` of its largest (or below `1e-12` outright, when
the whole spectrum is that small), the analogue of NONMEM's "R matrix
algorithmically singular", so the check applies at every `severity` the
warning reports: that grade measures how much the floor moved the *reported*
standard errors, not whether the model is identified.

The two thresholds are evaluated only when their input exists — a fit without a
covariance matrix has no condition number to test. Such a case lands in
`verdict.skipped` rather than failing or silently passing; pair the thresholds
with `require_covariance = true` to make them mandatory. `Strictness::none()`
turns every gate off for a "rank everything, report everything" run.

The predicates are also available on their own — `estimate_near_boundary`,
`stalled_at_init`, `max_abs_correlation` — for a report that prints the numbers
rather than the verdict.

## Assembling the inputs yourself

A caller that parses the model and reads the data itself (the R package, a
tool) has to do one step the file entry points do for it: **bind the model to
the data**. Two kinds of declaration have no value until the dataset is known:

- a data-driven level block, `theta NAME[COL, ...]`, whose level count is the
  set of combinations the data shows ([parameters](../model-file/parameters.qmd#data-driven-form-theta-namecol-...));
- a symbolic `[covariate_model]` statistic, such as `center = median`,
  `ref = mode` or `levels = auto`.

`bind_theta_levels` and `bind_covariate_stats` resolve them against the
population, after it is read and before `fit`. Both re-parse the model, so keep
the model text, and take the initial estimates and options from the re-parsed
model:

```rust
use ferx_core::api::{bind_covariate_stats, read_population_for};
use ferx_core::io::datareader::SelectionFilter;
use ferx_core::*;
use std::path::Path;

let model_text = std::fs::read_to_string("model.ferx").map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
let mut parsed = parse_full_model_file(Path::new("model.ferx"))?;
let opts = &parsed.fit_options;
let filter = SelectionFilter::from_opts(&opts.ignore_exprs, &opts.accept_exprs, &opts.ignore_subjects)?;
let (mut population, _) = read_population_for(
    &parsed.model, &parsed.covariate_decls, "data.csv", None,
    opts.iov_column.as_deref(), Some(&filter), &parsed.column_map,
)?;

// The binders return an `EngineError` (#1773); its `to_string()` is the message.
bind_theta_levels(&mut parsed, &model_text, &mut population).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
bind_covariate_stats(&mut parsed, &model_text, &population).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;

let result = fit(&parsed.model, &population, &parsed.model.default_params, &parsed.fit_options)?;
```

### A model or population left unbound

Both binders are no-ops for a model that declares neither, so calling them
unconditionally is safe. Skip `bind_theta_levels` on a level-block model and
`fit()` refuses it, naming the block. The simulate paths and `predict` report
the same problem as `E_THETA_LEVELS_UNBOUND`. The other half, a *bound* model
handed a population that was never bound, is `E_THETA_LEVELS_DATA_UNBOUND` on
`predict`, the simulate paths, `compute_npde_npd`, `predict_survival`,
`predict_categorical` and `fit`; one bound for other levels than the model's is
`E_THETA_LEVELS_DATA_MISMATCH` there, refused and never re-indexed (#1762). To
run a θ already laid out (a fit's, or the model's own), bind that population with
`bind_from_fit` and the bindings the θ was laid out on. To fit it, bind a fresh
parse with `bind_theta_levels`
([#1647](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1647)). To simulate with the model's own initial
estimates, bind a design the same way, on the population from
`read_population_for_simulation`. To simulate with a *fit's* θ, bind it against
the fit instead, as described
[below](#simulate-with-fit-theta).

### Binding a bound model again

A model already bound can be bound again, to other data, and binds as a fresh
parse of its text would. Each binder reads what the text declares, not what the
first data resolved it to: a level block declared `auto` takes the contrast the
new data resolves, and a `center = median` takes the new data's median. A binder
keeps the other half only while it still holds on the new data. The statistics
are kept only when the new population summarises to the same values. The level
layout is kept only when the population carries the level index columns and
shows exactly the bound levels, so the columns were written for that layout.
Otherwise that half is dropped, and the other binder binds it on the new data
([#1730](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1730)). A model bound
against a fit, described next, is the exception to all of this.

A layout that `bind_covariate_stats` keeps also keeps its contrast. A block
declared `auto` can resolve differently on data with the same levels, for
example with more subjects per study, and the statistics binder does not
re-resolve it. To re-bind both halves on new data, call `bind_theta_levels`
first, as the example does
([#1736](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1736)).

The other two steps are what the file entry points do besides binding: the
`[data_selection]` filter and the IOV column go to the reader. Leave either out
and the fit runs without that setting, and nothing warns you. `gradient` needs
no step: `fit` reads it from the options it is given, so a file's
`gradient = fd` takes effect here as it does from the file entry points, and an
SDE model runs on finite differences whatever it says
([#1613](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1613)). With both steps,
the example gives the same parameter vector and the same objective as
`run_model_with_data`, equal to the bit. The test suite pins that on a
level-block model, alone, with `gradient = fd` and with a `[data_selection]`
block. A caller that has a model *path* can use
`prepare_run(model_path, data_path)` instead, which does all of this and
returns the inputs without fitting.

### Simulating with a fit's θ: `bind_from_fit` {#simulate-with-fit-theta}

A fit's θ belongs to the model as it was compiled for the fit's data, and two
parts of that compilation come from the data. A level block's θ vector is laid
out by the levels the fit observed. A symbolic `[covariate_model]` centre
(`center = median` and friends) is the fit data's statistic. Binding a
simulation design with `bind_theta_levels` and `bind_covariate_stats`
re-derives both from the *design*. A design whose level combinations differ
from the fit's (a subset, a new time grid, another study, or only more subjects
per study, which can change the resolved contrast) reads the fitted values at
the wrong positions. A design of heavier subjects re-centres every covariate
factor on its own median. Neither is refused: the θ vector has the right
length, and the model is fully bound.

Bind the design against the fit's own bindings instead. The fit carries them:
`result.data_bindings` holds the level bindings and the covariate statistics
the fitted model was compiled from, and a `.fitrx` bundle saves and reloads
them, so the same code works on `load_fit(path)?.fit`
([#1621](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1621),
[#1619](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1619)):

```rust
use ferx_core::api::{bind_from_fit, read_population_for_simulation};
use ferx_core::estimation::uncertainty_samples::fitted_params_from_result;

// Continuing the example above (or with `result = load_fit(path)?.fit`).
let mut design_parsed = parse_full_model_file(Path::new("model.ferx"))?;
let (mut design, _) = read_population_for_simulation(
    &design_parsed.model, &design_parsed.covariate_decls, "design.csv", None,
    None, None, &design_parsed.column_map,
)?;
bind_from_fit(&mut design_parsed, &model_text, &mut design, &result.data_bindings)
    .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
let fitted_params = fitted_params_from_result(&result, &design_parsed.model)?;
let rows = simulate_with_seed(&design_parsed.model, &design, &fitted_params, 200, 1)
    .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
```

One call binds both halves. On the measured case, a design of the fit's
heavier half (WT median 80.6 against the fit's 70.85) simulates bit for bit
like the fitted model. Centred on its own median it moves the predictions by up
to 17%. After `bind_from_fit` or `layout_from_fit`, the model records that its
bindings are the fit's. A `bind_covariate_stats` call on it then changes
nothing, since the fitted θ was estimated against the fit's centres, not the
design's. `bind_theta_levels` refuses it, since the design's own levels would
read the fitted θ at other positions
([#1730](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1730)). A fit that
carries no bindings, such as a `.fitrx` saved before they were recorded, is
refused rather than re-bound on the design. Refit the model to record them.
This holds for a model already bound to other data too, such as one
`prepare_run` bound to a design. What the model needs is read from its text, so
the design's centres cannot stand in for the fit's, and a level block declared
`auto` takes the contrast the fit resolved, not the design's
([#1686](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1686)).
`bind_theta_levels_from_fit`, the earlier levels-only binder, is deprecated.

Each design record gets its level's index in the fit, and the model is re-parsed
with the fit's labels, groups and contrast, so its θ layout is the fit's. A
design level the fit never observed is refused, naming the block and every such
label: no θ was estimated for it, and any stand-in would be a modelling choice
made silently. On a block keyed on `TIME`, such as `PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME]`, this
means the design can only be simulated at the fit's observation times. A denser
VPC grid is refused, and so is a study the fit did not include. Levels match by
their label (`STUDY=7,TIME=4`), so a value differing from the fit's in its last
digit is a different level. The refusal names actions rather than functions,
because the R wrapper passes it through verbatim: simulate only the fit's
levels, or simulate the design on its own levels without the fit's θ. From
Rust, the second is `bind_theta_levels` on the design, with a θ for the levels
it discovers (the model's `default_params`, for example).

Bindings that a fit could not have written are refused too, since a `.fitrx`
stores them as editable data. That covers a level listed twice, a contrast
group split across non-adjacent levels, an unresolved `auto` contrast, a
contrast other than the one the block declares (`ref` and `sum_to_zero` free
the same number of θ, so a swap would otherwise read the fitted values under
the wrong convention), a missing covariate statistic, and one that no relation
reads.

#### The fit's layout without a population: `layout_from_fit` {#layout-from-fit}

`layout_from_fit(&mut parsed, &model_text, &result.data_bindings)` is the
model half of `bind_from_fit`. It lays the model out on the fit's bindings:
the same θ count, names, initial values, bounds and `FIX` flags. It writes
nothing to any population. Use it when you need the model's shape but have no
data to bind, for example to size a skeleton `FitResult` for SIR or a
standalone covariance step. `bind_from_fit` runs the same function, so the
two cannot disagree on a layout. It also refuses everything `bind_from_fit`
refuses, except a level the fit never observed, since there is no population
to look for one in
([#1703](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1703)). The model it
leaves in `parsed` is not ready to run on data with a level block: the block reads its
index columns from the population, and only `bind_from_fit` writes them.

#### The θ vector's length

Every `simulate*` entry point also refuses a θ vector whose length is not the
model's (`E_THETA_LENGTH`). Previously a short vector simulated plausible rows
from zeros past its end, and a long one dropped its tail
([#1614](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1614)). `predict`,
`predict_diag`, `predict_survival`, `predict_categorical` and
`stats::npde::compute_npde_npd` refuse it the same way; before, a short θ
predicted 0 ([#1615](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1615)).
`fit()` refuses initial parameters of the wrong θ length the same way; before,
a short θ fitted to a meaningless objective and a long one panicked
([#1764](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1764)).

#### The shape of Ω, σ and Ω~IOV~

The entry points that read random effects or residual errors — `fit()` (its
initial parameters), every `simulate*` and adaptive entry point,
`simulate_with_uncertainty`, `compute_npde_npd`, `run_sir()` and
`run_covariance()` — refuse an Ω, σ or Ω~IOV~ whose dimension is not the
model's (`E_PARAM_SHAPE`), as well as an Ω~IOV~ on a model with no κ and a
missing one on a model with κ. Previously a mis-sized block panicked, and a
long σ or a missing Ω~IOV~ ran to completion with the block silently ignored
([#1764](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1764)). An Ω or Ω~IOV~
that is not square is refused first, with its own message, even when its row
count matches the model; before, it panicked
([#1833](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1833)). `run_sir()`,
`run_covariance()` and `fitted_params_from_result()` check all three blocks of
the fit. `predict` and the survival predictors read none of the
three, so they do not check them. On `simulate*` a missing Ω~IOV~ keeps its
own message ([#1019](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1019)), and
`compute_npde_npd` keeps its documented fallback to κ = 0 for one. On
`run_sir()`, `run_covariance()` and `simulate_with_uncertainty` a fit with no
Ω~IOV~ is refused: before, they used the model's initial Ω~IOV~ in its place.
`fit()` returns these refusals as its message only, since its error is a
string.

`fitted_params_from_result()` refuses the same three Ω~IOV~ cases for a direct
caller, with the same code. It used to substitute the initial Ω~IOV~ for a
missing one, drop one on a model with no κ, and copy a mis-sized one unchecked
([#1789](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1789)). Its error type is
now `EngineError` instead of `String`.

### Level labels and values: `theta_level_map`, `theta_level_values` {#level-labels-values}

A bound level block's estimates are named after their combination, such as
`PLACEBO[STUDY=7,TIME=4]`. Under a sum-to-zero constraint one level is not a
free parameter, so it is absent from `FitResult::theta_names`.
`theta_level_map(&parsed.model)` returns every level, the dependent one
included, keyed by block name. Each label is the combination without the
block name (`STUDY=7,TIME=4`), in index order.

`theta_level_values(&parsed.model, &result.theta)` adds each level's value at
that θ, in the same order. Each `ThetaLevelValue` carries the `label`, the
`value`, and a `theta_index`. A free level's `theta_index` is `Some(k)`, its
position in `theta`, `theta_names` and the θ standard errors, so SEs can be
joined to it. A dependent level's is `None`. Its value is what the model
applies: the negated sum of its group's free θ under `sum_to_zero` and
`sum_to_zero_within`, and `0` for a `ref` reference level. The value is read
through the same evaluator the predictions use, never re-derived. The θ must be
laid out for that bound model, so pass the fit's own θ with the model it was
fitted with (or one rebound with `bind_from_fit`). A θ of the wrong
length is refused. Unbound blocks and counted `theta NAME[N]` blocks are left
out.

A block of 20 or more free coefficients is reported in its own compact section
instead of one entry per θ in the main table, by the console report,
`format_summary` and the fit YAML. `parameter_table`, `format_comparison`, the
CLI's post-fit θ list and the JSON result list every θ. The rule is public as
`ferx_core::io::output::compact_theta_blocks(&result.theta_names)`, which
returns each such block's name and θ index range; the threshold is
`THETA_BLOCK_COMPACT_MIN`. It counts free coefficients, not levels: a 21-level
`sum_to_zero` block (20 free) is compacted and a 20-level one (19 free) is not.
Call the function rather than comparing against the constant, so a wrapper
cannot drift from the writers.
